title: French Defense: the structure and the pawn breaks
outcomes: Says which pawn is the base and which the head of the French Advance chain, and which lever (the c-pawn or the f-pawn) attacks each
Says what must stand behind the f-pawn lever before it is playable, and what it opens for both sides
Counts the attackers and defenders of d4 before capturing, and picks the knight route that keeps the c1 bishop free
Explains why both c-bishops look bad by the pawn count and why only Black's is actually shut in

steps.caption: Black to move after 3.e5. White's pawns on d4 and e5 form a chain; so do Black's on f7, e6 and d5. Before any move, look at both chains. Which pawn holds each chain up, and which pawn would you attack to loosen White's?

claims.statement: The pawn on d4 defends e5 and no pawn defends d4, so d4 is the base of White's chain.
The pawn on f7 defends e6 and no pawn defends f7, so f7 is the base of Black's chain.

steps.prompt: Before reading on: which white pawn would you attack to loosen the chain, the front one or the back one? What do you think happens to the other pawn?

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** A pawn chain has a back and a front. Black has a lever against each end, and White has answers to both. By the end you can say which lever hits which pawn, what each needs before it works, and why the bad bishop is only part of Black's problem.

steps.caption: Lever one: the base. Step through the line and watch what holds e5 up. [I] White wins a pawn for the moment, but Black's pieces can usually take it back.

line.say: The first lever. The c-pawn attacks d4, the pawn at the back of White's chain.
White is a pawn up for a moment, but the chain is gone: no pawn stands behind e5.

claims.statement: After ...c5 a black pawn attacks d4, the base.
After dxc5 no white pawn defends the pawn on e5.

steps.text: **The second lever hits the head.** The f-pawn attacks e5, the front of White's chain. The c-pawn lever can come at once; the f-pawn lever needs help first. The contrast below starts from a position where ...f6 is playable and takes away Black's two supporting pieces, the knight on c6 and the bishop on d7. [I] The lever opens the f-file and loosens e6, so it pays only when Black's pieces also aim at e5.

steps.title: Is the head lever ...f6 clearly worse than the engine's choice?
steps.prompt: Predict for each position, then check. The second position takes away two black pieces; the third adds two kingside pawns. Which change matters, and which does not?

steps.caption: The head lever in a master line. Step through it: White develops, Black plays the lever, White castles before the file opens.

line.say: White develops and prepares to castle. The bishop keeps the d3 square free for the queen.
Black plays the lever. The f-pawn now attacks e5, which the pawn on d4 and the knight on f3 defend.
White finishes development first. The king leaves the e-file, which is about to open.

claims.statement: After 6...f6 a black pawn attacks e5.

steps.chapter: The head lever in a real game

steps.caption: Black takes the head of the chain and White recaptures with the knight. Say which defender of d4 is gone.

line.say: Black takes the head of the chain.
White recaptures with the knight, which keeps the pawn on d4 in place.

steps.caption: Black trades the knights and White recaptures with the pawn. Say what the break changed.

line.say: Black trades the knights; one defender of d4 is gone.
White recaptures with the pawn. The chain is gone, but White has a new pawn on e5 and a half-open d-file.

claims.statement: After the line the d-file is half-open for White and the f-file half-open for Black.
At depth 16 the engine rates the final position between 20 and 90 centipawns from White's side (100 = one pawn).

steps.text: **What strong players did.** In our master data (329,379 games, both players rated 2,500 or more, 2012 to 2026) 641 games reached the bishop move to e2 in this setup. Black chose the f-pawn lever in 132 of them and the knight move to e7 in 383. After White castled, Black captured on e5 in 114 of 125. These count choices; none is an evaluation.

steps.caption: What if White does not castle? Step through the other reply.

line.say: White takes the lever pawn at once, instead of castling.
Black recaptures with the knight: it lands on f6 with its first choice of squares, no longer pushed around by the pawn on e5.
White castles.

claims.statement: The knight stands on f6 after the recapture.

steps.caption: Black takes the base. Where does the position end up?

line.say: Black takes the base. With the head pawn gone, d4 no longer holds anything up.
White recaptures.
The bishop develops with an eye on the h2 pawn, and the position is close to level.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the final position between -40 and 30 centipawns from White's side (100 = one pawn).

steps.text: **What the break did.** [V] Castling first (the earlier line) leaves White a small edge, between 0.2 and 0.9 pawns at the end (depth 16). Taking the lever pawn at once (this line) is rated level, between -0.4 and +0.3. [I] So taking at once plays into Black's hands and gives up the pull on e5, while the quiet reply keeps it. A lever opens lines for both sides: Black gets the half-open f-file, White the half-open d-file.

steps.caption: Black to move after 5.Nf3. Count the pawns of each side that stand on the colour of that side's own bishops. Then count the squares each bishop can reach. The two counts do not say the same thing.

claims.statement: Five of Black's eight pawns stand on light squares, the colour of the c8 bishop.
Six of White's eight pawns stand on dark squares, the colour of the c1 bishop.
The bishop on c8 can move to one square.
The bishop on c1 can move to five squares.

steps.text: **Count first, then look.** By the pawn count both sides have a bad bishop: White's pawns on d4, e5 and c3 are dark, like the c1 bishop. But the c1 diagonal is open, so it can come out, while Black's c8 bishop has one square. [I] The count is a warning; the squares the bishop reaches are the proof.

steps.caption: Black can trade bishop activity for space. Step through it and count again.

line.say: Black closes the queenside and wins space for ...b5. But c4 is a light square, so one more black pawn now blocks the c8 bishop.

claims.statement: After ...c4 six of Black's eight pawns stand on light squares.
The bishop on c8 still has one square.
At depth 16 the engine rates the final position between 0 and 70 centipawns from White's side (100 = one pawn).

steps.prompt: [H] Black pushes the pawn to c4 and accepts a worse bishop for queenside space. Name one thing the bishop on c8 can no longer do after ...c4, and one thing Black gains. What would you need to see in a game to change your mind?

steps.text: **Count before you capture.** Black's pieces aim at the base d4, and White adds defenders. Count the pieces on each side first, then check their values and the order of captures: the side that runs out of recapturers loses the last piece. Watch both counts change as the pieces arrive, and notice which knight route keeps White's bishop on c1 free.

steps.caption: Count the attackers and defenders of d4 as the pieces arrive. First the knight route and the pawn trade.

line.say: The knight aims for f5, from where it will also attack d4.
White's knight heads for c2: it will defend d4 without blocking the bishop on c1.
Black trades the c-pawn for the d-pawn; the c-file is about to open.

steps.caption: A second knight attacks d4 and White's knight arrives on c2. Count again.

line.say: White recaptures with the pawn, which keeps the chain d4-e5.
A second knight attacks d4. Two black pieces now attack the base, two white pieces defend it.
The third defender arrives; the count is 2 against 3.

claims.statement: After 8...Nf5 two black pieces attack d4 (knights on c6 and f5).
After 8...Nf5 two white pieces defend d4 (knight on f3 and queen).
After 9.Nc2 three white pieces defend d4.
After cxd4 and cxd4 the c-file is open.
At depth 16 the engine rates the final position between -10 and 50 centipawns from White's side (100 = one pawn).

steps.caption: Same position, different bishop square. Count the defenders of d4 after this move.

line.say: The natural-looking bishop move. It stands on the d-file, between the queen and the pawn on d4.

claims.statement: After Bd3 two white pieces defend d4 (pawn c3 and knight f3); the queen is blocked.
After Be2 instead, three white pieces defend d4.

steps.text: **A tempting plan that costs White.** The pawn on e5 gives White space on the kingside, and a g-pawn push can gain a tempo against a knight on f5. [I] But it loosens White's own king. Black's counterplay is the f-pawn lever again, now with a knight on f5 and the c-file open for a rook. Step through the line, then read the engine's verdict.

steps.caption: Both ideas in one line. Black strikes at the head again and White castles. Step through it.

line.say: Black strikes at the head again.
White castles, the same reply as before.
Black takes.

claims.statement: After ...f6 a black pawn attacks e5.

steps.caption: White recaptures and keeps a pawn on e5; Black develops. What would you play now?

line.say: White recaptures with the d-pawn, keeping a pawn on e5.
Black develops the bishop and prepares to castle.

steps.caption: Now White gains a tempo with g4. The engine says level before the push and about 0.4 pawns for Black after it: gaining time is not the same as being better.

line.say: White gains time: the g-pawn attacks the knight on f5.

claims.statement: Before the push the engine's top choices are knight moves (Nfd4, Ne3 or Ncd4), depth 16.
Before the push the engine rates the position level, between -0.3 and +0.3 pawns (depth 16).
After g4 a white pawn attacks the knight on f5.
At depth 16 the engine rates the final position between -80 and -10 centipawns from White's side (100 = one pawn).

steps.text: **Typical mistakes.** [I] Black takes on d4 with a piece when the count is two against three (at least 3 pawns worse in our test). Smaller slips, about 0.3 to 0.4 pawns in the engine's view: White gives up the base by capturing on c5, or puts the bishop on d3 where it blocks the queen's defence of d4. Black pushes the f-pawn before any piece stands behind it. Try three unlabelled positions.

steps.prompt: [H] The French has two levers against two chain ends, each with its own timing. Name two pieces that should stand behind ...f6 before it is played, and write the count of d4 after Be2 and after Bd3.

steps.text: **Recap: what to remember.** The base is the pawn at the back of a chain, the head the pawn at the front. The c-pawn lever hits the base and can come at once; the f-pawn lever hits the head and needs pieces behind it. Count d4 before capturing. By pawn count both c-bishops are bad, but only Black's is shut in. Next: each side's setup.

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in two or three sentences, explain to a beginner why Black plays the c-pawn lever at once but waits to play the f-pawn lever. Say when each works and when it does not, give one example you could set up on a board, and one mistake to avoid. Self-check afterwards: did you say when it works and when it fails, give an example a beginner could set up, and name a mistake? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.
